{{Short description|Hypergraph representing intervals on real number lines}}
{{Distinguish|interval graph}}

In [[graph theory]], a '''{{mvar|d}}-interval hypergraph''' is a kind of a [[hypergraph]] constructed using [[Interval (mathematics)|intervals]] of [[real line]]s. The parameter {{mvar|d}} is a [[positive integer]]. The ''[[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]]'' of a {{mvar|d}}-interval hypergraph are the points of {{mvar|d}} disjoint [[Line (geometry)|lines]] (thus there are [[uncountably many]] vertices). The ''edges'' of the graph are {{mvar|d}}-[[tuple]]s of intervals, one interval in every real line.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Tardos|first=Gábor|date=1995-03-01|title=Transversals of 2-intervals, a topological approach|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf01294464|journal=[[Combinatorica]]|volume=15|issue=1|pages=123–134|doi=10.1007/bf01294464|doi-access=free|issn=0209-9683|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The simplest case is {{math|1=''d'' = 1}}. The vertex set of a 1-interval hypergraph is the set of real numbers; each edge in such a hypergraph is an interval of the real line. For example, the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] {{math|{ [−2, −1], [0, 5], [3, 7] } }} defines a 1-interval hypergraph. Note the difference from an [[interval graph]]: in an interval graph, the vertices are the intervals (a [[finite set]]); in a 1-interval hypergraph, the vertices are all points in the real line (an [[uncountable set]]). 

As another example, in a 2-interval hypergraph, the vertex set is the [[disjoint union]] of two real lines, and each edge is a union of two intervals: one in line #1 and one in line #2. 

The following two concepts are defined for {{mvar|d}}-interval hypergraphs just like for finite hypergraphs:

* A [[Matching in hypergraphs|''matching'']] is a set of non-intersecting edges, i.e., a set of non-intersecting {{mvar|d}}-intervals. For example, in the 1-interval hypergraph {{math|{ [−2, −1], [0, 5], [3, 7] },}} the set {{math|{ [−2, −1], [0, 5] } }} is a matching of size 2, but the set {{math|{ [0, 5], [3, 7] } }} is not a matching since its elements intersect. The largest matching size in {{mvar|H}} is denoted by {{math|''ν''(''H'')}}.
* A [[Vertex cover in hypergraphs|''covering'']] or a ''transversal'' is a set of vertices that intersects every edge, i.e., a set of points that intersects every {{mvar|d}}-interval. For example, in the 1-interval hypergraph {{math|{ [−2, −1], [0, 5], [3, 7] },}} the set {{math|{−1.5, 4} }} is a covering of size 2, but the set {{math|{−1.5, 1} }} is not a covering since it does not intersect the edge {{math|[3, 7]}}. The smallest transversal size in {{mvar|H}} is denoted by {{math|''τ''(''H'')}}. 

{{math|''ν''(''H'') ≤ ''τ''(''H'')}} is true for any hypergraph {{mvar|H}}. 

[[Tibor Gallai]] proved that, in a 1-interval hypergraph, they are equal: {{math|1=''τ''(''H'') = ''ν''(''H'')}}. This is analogous to [[Kőnig's theorem (graph theory)|Kőnig's theorem]] for [[bipartite graph]]s.

[[Gábor Tardos|Gabor Tardos]]<ref name=":0" /> proved that, in a 2-interval hypergraph, {{math|''τ''(''H'') ≤ 2''ν''(''H'')}}, and it is tight (i.e., every 2-interval hypergraph with a matching of size {{mvar|m}}, can be covered by {{math|2''m''}} points).

Kaiser<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kaiser|first=T.|date=1997-09-01|title=Transversals of d-Intervals|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009315|journal=[[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]|language=en|volume=18|issue=2|pages=195–203|doi=10.1007/PL00009315|issn=1432-0444|doi-access=free}}</ref> proved that, in a {{mvar|d}}-interval hypergraph, {{math|''τ''(''H'') ≤ ''d''(''d'' – 1)''ν''(''H'')}}, and moreover, every {{mvar|d}}-interval hypergraph with a matching of size {{mvar|m}}, can be covered by at {{math|''d''(''d'' − 1)''m''}} points, {{math|(''d'' − 1)''m''}} points on each line.

Frick and Zerbib<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Frick|first=Florian|last2=Zerbib|first2=Shira|date=2019-06-01|title=Colorful Coverings of Polytopes and Piercing Numbers of Colorful d-Intervals|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00493-018-3891-1|journal=[[Combinatorica]]|language=en|volume=39|issue=3|pages=627–637|doi=10.1007/s00493-018-3891-1|issn=1439-6912|arxiv=1710.07722}}</ref> proved a colorful ("[[Rainbow matching|rainbow]]") version of this theorem.
